Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I have to be on guard all the time
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'being followed or tracked' suggests an interpersonal/persecutory trauma context that is not supported by the other selected items and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal assault-style vigilance to sounds and sudden movements, which does not fit well with the stated trauma of toxic chemical exposure unless there is additional unreported violent context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies mistrust of others in a deceptive or persecutory sense; paired with 'being followed' it shifts the formulation toward interpersonal threat rather than contamination/exposure-related PTSD.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Avoid authority figures' is difficult to connect to the rest of the profile and to toxic chemical exposure specifically; no other items indicate authority-linked fear, blame, or trauma reminders involving uniforms/institutions.

vignette: Marta stood in the dimly lit control room of the chemical plant, the air thick with a greenish haze that clung to her lungs. The explosion that had erupted moments before left her coughing and short of breath; the acrid smell of bleach seeped through every crevice of her uniform. The sudden panic that seized her was not only physical—her chest tightened, her breath rattled—but also psychological: she could not stop replaying the flash of her own face, pale and trembling, as the toxic cloud engulfed the building. That instant became the fulcrum upon which every other distress would pivot, the single shock that would set the rest of her life in motion. Even months after the blast, the faint scent of antiseptic that swirls in a hospital corridor would snap her to a state of terror. The memory of the toxic fumes is so vivid that the smell alone sends her hand flying to cover her face, her fingers fumbling for the edges of her gloves. Each time her nose catches the sharp scent, she automatically tucks her hands over her mouth and nose, trying to block out the odor that feels like a living threat. The trigger is the smell, and the response is the covering of her face—a clear, repeated chain of trigger leading directly to her maladaptive strategy. Marta’s daily patrols are punctuated by the sudden clatter of a dropped toolbox or the distant rumble of a truck. Those unexpected sounds pull her breathing back to that ragged, shallow state she first experienced at the plant, and the echo of her own heart in her ears leaves her feeling as if the danger is still looming. The brief, involuntary breathlessness she experiences every time she hears a noise is a stark reminder of the threat that still lives in her mind, a threat that she has come to recognize and fear more than she once could have imagined. The same antiseptic odor does more than just make her cover her face; it also brings her memories to the surface. The recollection is not a complete picture, but a mosaic of disjointed images—her supervisor's voice, the hiss of the ventilation system, a splatter of green liquid on her uniform. The fragments refuse to stitch together, and each time she tries to recall, the vision dissolves before she can finish the story, leaving her feeling as if the memory is a present moment, never fully finished or past. The repeated failure of her mind to process those memories has fed into Marta’s own beliefs about the institutions that were supposed to protect her. The sense that the Department of Labor and the chemical safety regulators did nothing to safeguard her has taken root in her thoughts: she believes that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again because those emotions should have come from a system that failed. The institutional failure appraisals become the lens through which she views every new trigger, magnifying the danger she feels. Her conviction that her emotions are lost compels her to adopt more ways of shielding herself. When she thinks she might be vulnerable, Marta instinctively covers her face, a physical gesture that also signals to herself that she is not in a place where she can be seen, heard, or emotionally exposed. The protective gesture is her primary method of maintaining a safe emotional distance from people who represent authority, who might recall or remind her of the institutional failure she feels so strongly. Marta’s belief that any authority figure is a potential threat has led her to actively avoid people in uniforms, supervisors, and any official. The more she thinks institutions have let her down, the deeper her mistrust of those in power grows, and the stronger the sense of danger she feels whenever a uniformed person approaches. That mistrust has kept her from seeking help, even as the danger she feels intensifies. Because her negative appraisals drive her to push her memories away, she never fully processes the event. Each time a flash of the chemical plant hits her mind, she instinctively shoves the memory into a place she cannot access. The more she blocks, the more fragmented the memory becomes, and the more she feels trapped by the past. The fragmentation of the memory fuels Marta’s instinct to hide her face whenever the scent of bleach or the smell of hospital antiseptic catches her attention. Her avoidance of the very symbols of the event—her gloves, her face, the scent—creates a loop that only serves to keep her memory distant and unprocessed. The protective covering of her face keeps her from seeing the true emotional content of her memories. The more she hides, the less she can confront the reality of what happened, and the more she reinforces her belief that her emotions have been stolen or erased by the institutions that failed her. Marta’s continual avoidance and face-hiding isolate her from coworkers, from the normal camaraderie of the police precinct, and from the support she needs. The more she keeps herself at arm’s length, the stronger her conviction that institutions are untrustworthy and that she must remain on guard all the time. The isolation, in turn, reinforces her belief that she has lost her emotions and that the threat is real and ever-present. It is only in the last few months that Marta found herself unable to breathe in the cramped space of a closed crime scene because of a faint smell of bleach. The panic was so intense that she realized she could no longer carry out her duties safely; she could not protect the community she served without endangering herself. That crisis prompted her to reach out for professional help. She now fears that her job is at risk if she cannot manage the intrusive sensations, but she also hopes that therapy will let her reclaim the emotions she believes have been taken from her and restore a sense of safety that has long eluded her.
